The Indian Independence Movement was a centuries-long struggle by Indians against British colonial rule, culminating in independence in 1947. Led by political organizations like the Indian National Congress and figures like Mohandas Gandhi, the movement employed both constitutional reform and mass civil disobedience, ultimately forcing the British Empire to relinquish control. India's independence became a model for decolonization movements worldwide and demonstrated the power of nonviolent resistance against imperial power.

British colonial rule over India began in the eighteenth century through the East India Company's military conquest and commercial monopoly. It was formalized under Crown rule after the Indian Rebellion of 1857 to 1858, which established the British Raj as direct imperial governance. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885 by educated Indian elites, began as a constitutional reform movement seeking gradual Indian participation in government. After World War I, when British promises remained unfulfilled, it evolved into an independence movement.

Mohandas Gandhi emerged as the movement's foremost leader during the 1920s, championing Satyagraha—nonviolent resistance based on truth-force—boycotts of British goods, and mass civil disobedience campaigns that mobilized millions and changed anti-colonial strategy globally. Major campaigns included the Non-Cooperation Movement from 1920 to 1922, the Salt March in 1930 protesting the British salt monopoly, and the Quit India Movement in 1942 demanding immediate British withdrawal. Each campaign faced British repression but grew in scope and popular participation.

The independence struggle was not monolithic. Hindu-Muslim tensions and communal violence intensified during the 1940s, leading to the traumatic Partition of India in 1947 that created Pakistan, displacing millions and killing hundreds of thousands in communal riots. Indian independence in 1947 inspired and accelerated decolonization movements across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean, establishing a template for anti-imperial resistance through nonviolence and popular mobilization. India emerged as a major postcolonial power and leader of the Non-Aligned Movement. Post-independence India faced immense challenges in nation-building, Hindu-Muslim coexistence after Partition, integration of princely states, and transformation of a feudal agrarian society into a modern nation-state and democracy.
